title: KQFuzz: Knowledge-Guided Fuzzing for Quantum Libraries via Large Language Models
authors: Fuyuan Xia, Qixin Zhang, Chenhao Ying, Haojin Zhu, Shuai Wang, Yuan Luo, Pingchuan Ma, Yuxuan Du
abstract: As quantum computing continually improves, ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum libraries has become increasingly critical. To this end, many LLM-based fuzzing approaches towards quantum libraries have been proposed to uncover potential bugs. However, these methods still suffer from limitations such as insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, which hinder the progress of the quantum computing field. To address these challenges, we propose KQFuzz, a novel knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries. It leverages comprehensive codebase knowledge to ground LLM-based test generation, synergizing this with fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations to explore complex execution paths and trigger potential bugs. Firstly, KQFuzz introduces a novel prompting scheme tailored to quantum programs, which strategically incorporates knowledge of the codebase to efficiently generate high-quality quantum seed programs. Moreover, we develop evaluation and mutation strategies to handle the generated seed programs, facilitating efficient fuzzing execution while further enriching the diversity of the resulting test cases. We implement KQFuzz and conduct fuzzing on three popular quantum libraries, including Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, with coverage improved by up to 18.44%. During the development of KQFuzz, we discovered 13 bugs, all of which have been confirmed and 12 have already been fixed by the developers.
summary: This paper introduces KQFuzz, a novel knowledge-guided fuzzer designed to test the reliability of quantum computing libraries. It enhances LLM-based testing by incorporating deep codebase knowledge and advanced mutation strategies. The resulting framework significantly improves bug discovery and code coverage across major quantum frameworks.
main_problem: Ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum libraries is critical, but existing fuzzing methods lack flexibility and efficiency.
main_result: KQFuzz significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving code coverage by up to 18.44% and discovering multiple confirmed bugs in major quantum libraries.
method: The authors propose KQFuzz, a knowledge-guided fuzzer that uses codebase knowledge to ground LLM test generation, combined with fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations.
model_or_system: The work targets software implementations of quantum computation within popular libraries like Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq, which operate on the quantum circuit model involving gates and qubits.
key_observables: Code coverage improvement (up to 18.44%), bug discovery rate (13 bugs found), code validity, and execution time/token consumption.
important_parameters: The two-level mutation strategy involves parameter-level and gate-level structural mutations; the fitness function incorporates gate diversity and entangled qubits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that increased output token count in KQFuzz represents meaningful semantic content leading to higher quality tests, rather than mere redundancy.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the scope of different fuzzer types; Figure 3 shows empirical comparison of validity rates for classical vs. quantum domains; Table 8 and 9 detail computational cost analysis across various stages and models.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the limitations of current fuzzing techniques, then introduces KQFuzz with its knowledge corpus construction (static metadata, API associations, semantic models), followed by detailed descriptions of the generation/mutation strategies. It presents empirical results comparing against baselines on multiple quantum libraries and concludes with an efficiency analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on software testing rather than physical dynamics, the rigorous validation techniques developed for quantum circuit execution are crucial for building reliable simulation tools necessary for studying complex many-body physics or open quantum systems.
